design.quote: We conducted the first comprehensive systematic review and meta‑analysis of the side effects of MDMA‑AP across indications.
design.text: Systematic review and meta‑analysis of side effects of MDMA‑assisted psychotherapy

findings.quote: MDMA‑AP was associated with increased odds of any side effect during medication sessions (OR = 1.67, 95%CI (1.12, 2.49)) and in the 7 days following (OR = 1.59, 95%CI (1.12, 2.24)) relative to control conditions.
findings.text: MDMA‑AP increased the odds of any side effect during medication sessions (OR = 1.67, 95% CI 1.12–2.49) and in the 7 days after (OR = 1.59, 95% CI 1.12–2.24) compared with control.

findings.quote: Participants treated with MDMA‑AP also had 4.7 greater odds of anxiety and 4.8 greater odds of jaw clenching during medication sessions relative to placebo participants.
findings.text: MDMA‑AP increased the odds of anxiety (OR = 4.7) and jaw clenching (OR = 4.8) during medication sessions compared with placebo.

findings.quote: MDMA‑AP participants had 3.5 times greater odds of experiencing any TEAE compared with placebo participants. They also had increased odds of muscle tightness, decreased appetite, nausea, excessive perspiration, feeling cold, restlessness, dilated pupils, jaw clenching, uncontrolled eye movements, feeling jittery, non‑cardiac chest pain/discomfort, blurred vision, and chills.
findings.text: MDMA‑AP increased the odds of any treatment‑emergent adverse event (OR = 3.5) and of specific symptoms such as muscle tightness, decreased appetite, nausea, excessive perspiration, feeling cold, restlessness, dilated pupils, jaw clenching, uncontrolled eye movements, feeling jittery, non‑cardiac chest pain, blurred vision, and chills compared with placebo.

limits.quote: The overall evidence on MDMA‑AP, however, consists of a relatively limited number of studies with highly selective samples (i.e., most people volunteering for these studies were excluded from participation).
limits.text: The evidence is based on a limited number of studies with highly selective samples, limiting generalizability.

sources.title: Beyond ecstasy: Alternative entactogens to 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine with potential applications in psychotherapy

design.quote: The last two decades have seen a revival of interest in the entactogen 3,4-methylenedioxy-N-methylamphetamine (MDMA) as an adjunct to psychotherapy, particularly for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder.
design.text: Review paper examining alternative entactogens to MDMA

findings.quote: One of the few drug-discrimination studies performed in rats using benzofurans found that 5-APB, as well as 6-APDB (the 2,3-dihydro isomer of 6-APB), fully substituted for MDMA in rats trained to discriminate MDMA from vehicle.
findings.text: In rats, 5‑APB and 6‑APDB fully substituted for MDMA in a drug‑discrimination task.

findings.quote: The fact that users report the effects of 6-APB as having a slightly more psychedelic character than MDMA, particularly at higher doses, is not entirely surprising, since structurally it is an analogue of MDA, whose R-enantiomer has been shown to produce more psychedelic effects than its S-enantiomer.
findings.text: Users report that 6‑APB has a slightly more psychedelic character than MDMA, especially at higher doses.

findings.quote: The onset of effects is generally described as more gradual and less ‘forced’ than the onset of MDMA. The duration of the entactogenic effects is also described as being longer (around 5–8 h for all four of the benzofurans as opposed to 3–6 h for MDMA) with greater mental clarity than MDMA.
findings.text: The entactogenic effects of 6‑APB last about 5–8 h, longer than the 3–6 h duration of MDMA, with a more gradual onset.

limits.quote: While little is known about their long-term neurological effects, they generally seem to be tolerated better than MDMA by users.
limits.text: Little is known about the long-term neurological effects of benzofurans.
